segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: A quick warning-- there are curse words that are unbeeped in today's episode of the show. If you prefer a beeped version, you can find that at our website, thisamericanlife.org.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Aviva DeKornfeld, sitting in for Ira Glass. So there's this recording I heard a couple months ago. And when I heard it, I could not believe it existed. I'd never heard anything like it. It was recorded at a hotel bar at the Vancouver airport by this woman named Vienna Luke. She'd arranged to meet with this guy, Justin, who she hadn't seen in almost a decade. She's sitting at a table. She orders a tea, sipping it slowly while she waits for him to arrive. She's wired for sound.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Every so often, I'm kind of glancing to where the hostess desk is. And then I see Justin walk in across the restaurant, and he's asking the hostess where I'm sitting. Or he's saying, I'm meeting someone here.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Oh, I think the guy's here. Dang, he looks exactly the same.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: And I say, dang, he looks exactly the same. Like, he is exactly who he has always been. He has not changed. And he has no idea what's coming because he doesn't know I'm different.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna's got a hidden recorder in her purse sitting on the table and another recorder hidden in her bra. There are three cops in plain clothes sitting at tables around her, and a bunch more upstairs in a hotel room. Justin spots Vienna, walks over to her table, and Vienna jumps right in, with a nervous preamble.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK, so, [CHUCKLES] yeah, obviously, I haven't really wanted to do this for quite some time. And-- but I actually have a notebook today, and I wrote notes because I want to make sure that I cover off everything that I want to. Whew, and we're going to take this at my pace. And--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Can I just ask before you start, are you recording this?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: OK. It wouldn't matter to me because I feel this is your information, and you do with it whatever you want.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna is secretly recording because she's pretty sure that years ago, Justin assaulted her. But she doesn't know for sure. She has big gaps in her memory from that night. Memory gaps are pretty common in cases of sexual assault, which makes for a horrible situation because the one person who could clear things up and tell you what happened, the person who assaulted you, is the least likely person to talk to you and tell you the truth. Because why would they?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: In Vienna's case, though, the man, Justin, actually agreed to sit down with her and talk about everything, to answer all of her questions in detail. I think most of us walk around with blank spots in our lives, small ones, big ones. And a lot of the time, you just give up on trying to get answers, accepting that you're just going to wonder forever. So what's it like to actually get all the answers you spent so long wondering about? And where does that leave you? Most of our show today is going to be the story of this recording. It's really remarkable. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, Known Unknowns. So Vienna is at this hotel bar at the Vancouver airport, wearing that hidden recorder. And just a heads-up, before we start, this story includes a bunch of explicit details and references to sexual assault.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The man in the recording, which we'll get to in a minute, his name is Justin. He's a father of four boys, a veterinarian, though he has a sort of finance guy look about him-- close-cropped hair, symmetrical face, wouldn't look out of place in a Patagonia vest. Vienna's a fitness instructor and mom to two kids. She's warm and sensitive and loves an inspirational quote. She and Justin are actually related. Justin is Vienna's brother-in-law, her oldest sister, Sunny's, husband.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I met him when I was 10. And yeah, he felt like an older brother. And I'd only had sisters, so having a brother was exciting. And I thought he was charming. I mean, he was very self-assured. And I guess I thought that was cool.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: For 14 years, Vienna has wanted to ask Justin about one night from when she was 20 and he was 31. She was living with Sunny and Justin, up in their small northern Canadian town, where they'd moved after they got married. And one day, when Sunny was away, Justin asked Vienna--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, do you want to get drunk to experience what it's like to be drunk in a safe place? That was the premise.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Which sounded reasonable to Vienna. She and her family were evangelical Christians. She went to church every Sunday. Justin was part of the leadership. And she'd had friends in the church who'd gotten drunk for the first time under a similar arrangement. So Justin makes Vienna a few mixed drinks to try-- a strawberry daiquiri, a piña colada, some kind of Kahlua thing, exactly the kind of drinks you might order for yourself if you were 20 and didn't like the taste of alcohol.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: He's got music playing, like country music. And after I'd had a couple sips, he was dancing with me, two-stepping with me. And I feel like, already then, I was starting to feel a little bit woozy. And then I basically lose feeling in my legs and collapse on the ottoman. And I'm like, oh, my goodness, if this is what it feels like to be drunk, this is rough. Why do people do this?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna passes out. A little while later, she comes to in her bedroom, which is in the basement. She has no clue how she got there from the living room upstairs. And she only has one more brief memory from the evening. Warning for the listeners-- this next detail might be upsetting.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The one moment Vienna woke up, she remembers having an out-of-body experience, looking down at herself, seeing Justin taking off her underwear. The next morning, Vienna wakes up with a stomach ache and a bad feeling. She tells Justin that she's not sure exactly what happened, but that she thinks he should tell Sunny. He brushes her off, saying there's no need to tell her. It'll just trouble her. And besides, nothing happened anyway.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I'm like, OK, yeah, that's what I've been trying to tell myself, too, as this memory comes up.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You're almost hoping for that answer--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, no.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: --to be like, OK, it's nothing, right? It's nothing.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, it's nothing. I mean, even in the moment, I remember telling myself, he's taking off my underwear because I must have vomited. I must have gotten--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This must be a brotherly, familial act.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, like, oh, he's just changing my clothes because I threw up on myself. So I'd say things like that to myself. And then I'd be like, but why would he have to change my underwear?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So this night happens. And Vienna has to decide, does she tell her family? And if she does, what exactly is she even telling them if she doesn't know any of the details? Vienna's family is one that makes a point to spend a lot of time all together-- Vienna's parents, her two sisters, and her. Vienna's the baby. She grew up particularly close with her oldest sister, Sunny, Justin's wife. Sunny is 10 years older than Vienna, so she was more like a second mom to her. Sunny would dote on her, read Junie B. Jones to her at night. She painted a mural of farm animals on her bedroom wall. When Vienna got older, they'd bake chocolate chip cookies together.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But for months after that night, Vienna doesn't tell anyone about what happened, until at the end of a family vacation, Vienna's middle sister, Shawnessy, notices Justin pull Vienna into this long hug, a hug that looked too intimate to her eye. So Shawnessy, being the loud, confrontational one in the family, corners Vienna and badgers the truth out of her.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna stumbles through a partial explanation, saying Justin gave her alcohol, but she can't bring herself to mention the one thing she remembers about the night, about him taking off her underwear. But even without that detail, something about the way Vienna was talking, her body language, Shawnessy thought, Justin must have done something inappropriate. So she convinces Vienna to tell their parents. And Vienna tells them what she told Shawnessy. Vienna's parents are very surprised she got drunk. Vienna's dad calls Justin to get answers about what exactly happened.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin, of course, downplays everything, saying Vienna just drank too much, that's all. When Justin's wife, Sunny, hears about all this, she shuts down entirely. Sunny's not her real name, by the way.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: My sister didn't want to know anything and basically pretended like it didn't happen. I think everyone was just so confused. They didn't know what to do with it. And at the end of the day, people just-- they just want the family to be together. So pretty much, it was just like life as usual after that. And I would have had to see him at the next family thing.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: There's a terrible ordinariness to sexual violence. I don't know any woman who hasn't, at some point, wondered if a man was going to hurt her. What's extraordinary about Vienna's story, though, is how she chose to respond to what happened to her. But that doesn't happen for years, because for almost a decade, Vienna tried to continue on like normal. She's naturally a peacemaker, and pushing the issue with Justin just seemed like it would cause problems for everyone.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Plus, at this point, Vienna is depressed, operating on autopilot, and didn't have the wherewithal to force her family to confront a thing she wasn't ready to deal with herself. So instead, she went to university, spent time with her family, tried to figure out what she wanted to do with her life, but she couldn't shake the unsettled feeling she'd had ever since the night Justin gave her alcohol. And eventually, the uncertainty about what happened to her that night became this kind of torture, just question marks looping nonstop in the back of her brain as she went about daily life.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Then, in 2014, seven years after the night Justin assaulted her, Vienna's oldest sister Sunny discovered that Justin was having an affair-- multiple affairs, actually. This news rocked their community. Everyone had seen him as this wholesome family man, an elder in the church. Sunny ended up taking Justin back after a couple months. But for Vienna--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: It was this affirmation that he was capable of not being a nice guy. I finally believed myself.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And what was it exactly that you believed?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: That he had done something to me, that something had happened.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So Vienna cut Justin out. Shawnessy did as well. She'd always believed Justin had done something to Vienna, even though at this point, Vienna still hadn't told her the detail about the underwear. Both refused to be in the same room as Justin. Vienna's parents positioned themselves as a kind of see-no-evil Switzerland in the middle of this newfound estrangement, with Vienna and Shawnessy on one side and Justin and Sunny on the other. They felt uneasy about what they knew, but they didn't know how else to handle it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And so the entire family structure was reorganized to accommodate this vague, undiscussed thing that happened. For a family that loves spending time together, this meant no more holidays, no more family vacations. They all settled into a painful, awkward, strange, new normal for a few years, until one night, Vienna called her middle sister, Shawnessy, and said, I'm finally ready to figure out what happened to me. It had been 12 years since the night.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: In order to go to the police, Vienna and Shawnessy figure they need more evidence than Vienna's one memory of the night. So together, they make a list of everyone they knew Justin had been close with at the time of the assault, but wasn't close to anymore-- old coworkers, former friends. They figured, maybe he had talked to someone about what he'd done. Vienna didn't want to talk to any of these people herself. So Shawnessy calls roughly a dozen people, including one of Justin's former employees at the vet clinic he ran.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: And she says, I know why you're calling. He drugged your sister. And continues to tell my sister everything-- like, what she knows, that they were working in the back one day in the clinic, and he says, if you were giving whatever drug it was to a human, how much would you give them to make sure they were out?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Another former employee told Shawnessy that one day, the receptionist at the clinic was looking for something on the work computer and accidentally came across pictures of Justin with a naked woman who might have been Vienna. The woman's face wasn't visible. Some of the pictures were selfies Justin took, leaning against the woman's body.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: With those two pieces of information about the drugs and the pictures, Vienna and Shawnessy go to the police. Most sexual assault allegations that get reported, they never go anywhere. But Vienna gets extraordinarily lucky by getting the ear of a cop named Joelle LaChance, who's made tricky sexual assault cases her life's work. She's like one of those cops on a TV show whose secret sauce comes down to "she just really gives a shit." She used her vacation days to fly places for this case. She was late to her own sister's funeral because she was helping set up Vienna's Vancouver recording.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The idea of going to the police more than a decade after an assault with only one memory of what happened and hearsay from a couple former acquaintances and being taken seriously seems unimaginable. But that is what happened. Joelle ropes the undercover police team in to work with Vienna on her case, and they come up with a plan. For years, since Vienna first distanced herself from Justin, he had been emailing her periodically, asking her to return to the family. Vienna never responded to those emails.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But now, with the help of the police, she crafted a response, saying, basically, I'm willing to move past this, but in order for me to do that, I need you to tell me what happened that night. Justin writes back and says very clearly that he sexually assaulted her. Vienna thinks, OK, that was easy. We got him. But the police say they need more concrete evidence, something undeniable. A lawyer in court could argue that someone other than Justin had written that email to Vienna. And they needed specifics about what exactly he did.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So Vienna writes Justin again, saying, we need to meet in person, and you need to tell me the details of what happened. That's the only way I'll be able to move forward. Justin, miraculously, agrees. Vienna thinks it's because he figured he would get to be the hero if he could be the one to reunite the family. Justin offers to fly to Vancouver, where Vienna lives. So they decide to meet at the airport.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The cops picked the airport because even though they figured Justin wasn't likely an active threat to Vienna, they knew that if he had just walked off an airplane, there was no way he could have a weapon on him. And Vienna liked the airport idea, too. It felt comfortingly anonymous. In preparation for the meeting, the lead undercover cop spent a couple of days training Vienna on how to get usable information out of Justin.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: So the day I did training, I brought in my notebook, and he was like, whoa, this is so weird. You have a notebook. Nobody brings a notebook, because usually--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Wait, why not?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Because, usually, he's working with-- he's like, you are very different than the undercover people I usually work with, which, not to stereotype, but many of them are criminals that he's--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Like he's flipped them, and then they're going to work against--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yes, yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: --their former--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: So a bunch of the stuff we were going through in this contract, he's like, this isn't going to apply to you, but you can't commit any other crimes throughout this operation. He's like that.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And you're like, no problem.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So Vienna, A+ student with her little notebook, writes down everything she needs to get from Justin. And then she and the undercover cop role-play so she can practice pressing Justin when he tries to give her evasive non-answers. And a few weeks later, Vienna heads to the Vancouver airport.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I feel like I came here today, or know I came here today, wanting you to give me details on what happened. So I hope that you're ready to tell me the actual facts today.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Well, the things that I learned is that when there's disclosure, it's traumatic. And the best way is to have it all happen at once. So I don't want there to be any amount of information that has to be disclosed at a different point in time. This is the time. So you will get everything you need from me today. Because it will be more traumatic for you if you had to do it again.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin uses this bizarre therapy speak all throughout their conversation. Several years before this meeting, Justin went to counseling for sex addiction, and it seems like that's where he picked this up, this language that allows him to simultaneously acknowledge that something happened to Vienna, while also distancing himself from it. It's like he's saying, I can help you heal from this, while totally ignoring the fact that he's the reason she needs to heal in the first place.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: So throughout that night-- and I don't mean to go into other things. This whole objectification of women in our culture right now is what had happened for me in that time. And for some reason, I had a line drawn. I wasn't going to touch you in a sexual way.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK, but you're not actually telling me what happened.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No, I know. Sorry. And it's just sort of the rules before I start. So the rule for myself, everything that happened, was on this side of that line for me.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: The rules before you started what?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Before that night started. And again, I wouldn't say that they were even pretty thought-out rules and stuff.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, OK, let's get back to the night and what actually-- tell me what happened.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You're so impressively uncompromising in the tape. And every time he tries to stray and talk about the broader issue of objectification of women, you force him right back to the topic at hand.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I feel like I went into it with a mentality of, like, I cannot fail. I can't-- this is my one chance. I can't mess this up. It wasn't even an option. I remember my coach, my undercover cop, saying, he's going to try to make light of this. He's going to try to pull you off track. And you just have to keep bringing the focus back.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Tell me what happened.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: OK. I encouraged you to drink alcohol.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: You had never been drunk.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Were you drinking with me?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I don't remember that.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I didn't drink very much because I didn't want to be drunk.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I had done that in advance, setting this up as an opportunity for you to see what it was like to be drunk.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, yes, that's what you told me.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: But that's not what happened.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I remember that you laid down on the ottoman on your back.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Oh, I did not lay down. I lost feeling in my legs. And that's not what happens when someone gets drunk. [LAUGHS] So are you going to tell me what you did, or am I-- yeah, I didn't just lose feeling in my legs for nothing. And I've been drunk since.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right. I put something in one of the drinks. I was nervous about it, and I didn't know how much. And so I was cautious. And it was-- I can't imagine that it did anything to you. But maybe the combination is what did it. But I did put something in one of the drinks.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: And what was it?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I'm not sure if it was Valium or if it was Ketamine.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: You're not sure? Well, that doesn't make me feel like--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I know that I had both there.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Do you know how much you gave me?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No, I don't. It wasn't something that I'd done before, so I didn't know how much was appropriate. But I certainly didn't want to hurt anybody. I didn't want to hurt you. I remember you on your back on the ottoman. And you started--

segments.speaker: Waiter
segments.text: You guys OK with everything?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: We're good. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin's talking to a waiter here, who's asking if they have everything they need. I don't have anything smart to say about this. I just think it's insane to have to interact with a waiter while in the middle of a conversation like this.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: You were throwing up, so I helped you down the stairs to your bedroom. There was vomit on your clothing. And so I helped you out of your clothes. That's an odd way to phrase that. And the pictures that I took during that time were of you on the bed.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna now presses Justin for specifics about the pictures, just as the undercover cop instructed. She needs to get Justin to corroborate the fact that he gave her drugs, took off her clothes, and took pictures of her, with as many details as possible.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: How many photos did you take?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Was I wearing anything in any of them?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Can you describe them for me?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: There's a picture of you on your stomach from above. There's a picture of you on your back, showing your chest. There's a full-body picture of you from above with you laying on your back. I took a picture of us, like a selfie, at the time, of you on your back with me, with my head down close to your chest.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I took a picture of you on your side with my penis close to your face. But I never touched you with it. But there, again, none of the pictures-- I don't know if these details are important to you. Your legs are never open for any of those shots. I don't have any pictures of your genitalia.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: So the pictures were from the belly button up?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No, from the waist down as well, but only from the front and closed leg.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: It's only from the front because you had a line drawn.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I wasn't going to position you--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: With my legs open.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right. I had those pictures for a while afterwards. I was always disappointed that I didn't have a picture of the vagina. But I was never willing to position you to get one.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: If we take Justin at his word, it tells us something interesting, which is how he lives with what he's done. He's come up with a story he can tell himself so that he's still a good person because there are lines he drew and rules he set that he stayed on the right side of. I suspect that's why he agreed to talk to Vienna at all, and why there isn't a shred of remorse in his voice, because he doesn't really think of himself as a guy who did anything worth apologizing for.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Of course, just to say, for the rest of us who live in the real world, drugging your sister-in-law, stripping off all her clothes, and taking naked pictures of her for later use, none of that is anywhere close to being on the right side of any line.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So Justin has his justifications. But then there's some stuff that he has a really hard time explaining, try as he might. Listen to how he dodges this very simple question.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: What was your intent? Why did you take the pictures?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Sorry. I had a tough time talking about this and staying on top of going into the greater issue with pornography.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, but it's about you, and it's about me. So stick to it as much as you can.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Because it was you that looked at them, not the greater world that has--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No, I know.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: --problems with pornography.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: It's just the issue of pornography, just having pornography, right? Like, if you go around to computers, go door to door and start pulling computers apart, you'll find pornography on most of them.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, hopefully not a person's sister-in-law, but you know.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This is what got me in the recording, the way Vienna is like a prosecutor, quick and sharp and relentless, except she's cross-examining her own perpetrator. Like so many survivors, it took Vienna a long time to classify what happened to her as sexual assault. And that's in part because of who the perpetrator was-- her cool, charming, churchgoing brother-in-law, family.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But one of the reasons she's putting herself through this meeting with Justin is also family. The way she sees it, recording this conversation is her best chance at getting through to her sister, Sunny. Vienna hates how distant she and Sunny have become, how estranged. Sunny and her kids will visit Vienna and Shawnessy once or twice a year, but there's none of the intimacy they used to have, because Vienna's never gotten to have an open, honest conversation with Sunny about what happened to her.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The one time they came close was back when Sunny discovered Justin's affairs. She finally called Vienna and asked her about the night Justin got her drunk. And Vienna tried to tell her, but she said, pretty quickly, she realized Sunny didn't really want to understand. She was more there on behalf of Justin, as a kind of spokesperson. She kept defending him, saying things like, you don't understand. He was exposed to pornography when he was a kid. He had a sex addiction. He's a victim himself. It went nowhere.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But with this recording, Sunny would finally hear the truth about what happened. And then she might leave Justin once and for all. That was Vienna's hope.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Who saw them? I mean--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So Vienna is now about an hour into her hour and a half long conversation with Justin. And you can hear, the way Justin's speaking to her, that he still playing this knowing authority. And Vienna is sitting across from him like, I'm not who you think I am. I don't defer to you.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I kind of don't believe that you just took pictures of me naked.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: So, I guess, the reason that I wanted to draw that distinction between sexual contact and non-sexual contact is because there was contact that I felt was-- I remember I felt really close to you at that time. So I laid down beside you, and I put my arm around you, but I was careful that I didn't touch your breasts when I put my arm around you because that--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: But--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: --would be sexual.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: --you wrote in the email that you sexually assaulted me, [LAUGHS] which, yeah, so at what point--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I think of taking pictures of you as sexual assault.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: But--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Right. I masturbated twice. And it was between that I laid down with you. And so I was on-- after you have sex, there's a window of time where you're not ready to have sex again. And so it was during that time that I was laying beside you, spooning you, but just spooning you. And so I may have been up against you. My penis may have been in around your rear end, around your legs. But it wasn't-- I've always worried that there would have been some degree of mess. And you would have thought that potentially I had raped you.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK. After you masturbated, where did you--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: On you.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK, so that would be in the pictures.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Did you have to ask any questions as part of the investigation that you personally would rather not know?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: No. Yeah, I wanted to hear everything. Not wanted to, but I think when you spend so many years not knowing, yeah, it feels like just being unsettled for years and years and years, and the unknowns plague you. And I believed that if I had the pieces, that things would make sense to me.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Is that what happened?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, I mean, ultimately, when I say make sense, I mean, that night changed who I was fundamentally, down to my core. It changed me as a person. So actually getting some details on what happened made me realize that I wasn't crazy, that feeling so low, that that was normal based on what had happened.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The one memory Vienna has from the night of Justin taking off her underwear, it had taken years for her to tell anyone about it. It felt too shameful, too private. But now, she brings it up with Justin directly.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Did you do anything else to me? Did you go down on me?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I did not touch or see your genitalia.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, you did see it because you took off my underwear.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No, I--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: You removed my underwear.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I know, but that was a closed leg, slide them down. That wasn't a--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I never positioned you in a way that I could see.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Because I definitely came to with my shorts and underwear coming off and wondered why, if I was vomiting, I would need my underwear taken off. So yeah, I feel like you didn't just-- you didn't just stop there.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: There was no contact. You know that line that I talk about that I didn't want to cross, that I wasn't willing to cross?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, but you did cross it.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I know. I know.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: You absolutely crossed it. So I feel like it's really important for me to know if you did have sex with me for the first time--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I did not.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: --because, obviously, I was a virgin.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: The only time my penis came anywhere near your vagina was when I was soft.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Jordan's just calling me.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Hey.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: So when I say Jordan's just calling me, it's not Jordan.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Jordan is Vienna's partner.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: It's actually RCMP upstairs calling me.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: RCMP, Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Something was wrong with the transmission, and they'd missed large chunks of the conversation. So while Vienna was dutifully working through her checklist of questions, the cops upstairs were on edge. But Vienna didn't know that at the time.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: And I take the call, and I just go a couple steps away. There is a fireplace there in the restaurant, and I kind of step over closer to this fireplace. And I'm kind of like, oh, hey, what's up? And upstairs is like, have you got everything? How are you doing down there? And I'm like, I think I've got everything. But maybe I'm not going hard enough for some details. So you want me to kind of push, push in, go a little harder?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I'm going to give you a chance to tell me the truth.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I did not have sex with you. I guarantee you 100% that did not happen.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: You were already going there. Yeah, I just don't know why you would have stopped, you know?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I could have done anything I wanted.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah, exactly.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Why would I admit that I put drugs in the drink and then not admit that I had sex with you if I had?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Because you can justify that to yourself? I don't know.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: So in my--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Because it makes you feel better, even though you think maybe drugs are really bad. But it's less of an evil in your mind to be like, oh, just drugs, but rape is like-- you know?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I wanted you to not even know that anything had happened. Does that make sense?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: No, say--

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Can you understand that I would walk into that and hope that I could take pictures of you, go through the evening, and have you wake up the next day, and never know that any of it happened?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Oh, of course, you'd want that.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: V, when I look at the future, when I look at your family and my family and your parents and all of that, that's all that's at stake here right now.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Why would I not come clean on that if it wasn't?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, maybe you feel like you can get it without giving that up. For me, that's what I need you-- I need you to admit to that. [LAUGHS] You're not going to.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: I can't, V. That's a lie.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: It really would be a lie if I told you right now that I had done that. It would be a lie.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna's made it through her whole checklist of questions. So she asked Justin one last thing before she wraps up.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Is there anything that I'm not asking and you're not disclosing?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: No reason for me to disclose this, but I took pictures of you at other times.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: But it wasn't with you. It was through your window.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin's saying he took pictures of Vienna at other times, too, through her window.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: OK. Which window?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Your downstairs window.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Well, I lived with you at two separate locations.

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Both of them.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: So both of them. So how many pictures of me have you or did you have?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: 8, 10 pictures. They were blurry. They weren't good quality.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: How many occasions did you do this on?

segments.speaker: Justin
segments.text: Three or four.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin just admitted to a whole other crime that Vienna and the cops hadn't even intended to get out of him. And he does it in his detached, neutral, unapologetic way.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's glaring that in the whole hour and a half long conversation you guys had, he never says sorry.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: No, absolutely. There's definitely, like, yeah, no remorse.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Would it have meant anything to you for him to apologize?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I mean, if he was capable of apologizing and if it actually meant something, then, yeah, I would have taken it. But I don't believe he's capable.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I guess, thank you for coming down here and for meeting with me and for, I feel like-- well, for finally being honest. Because let's face it, you've had 14 years.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna spends an excruciating few minutes trying to flag down a waiter to pay for her tea. Before he leaves, Justin hands Vienna a goodie bag of cookies that Sunny had baked for her, along with a bunch of carrots from their garden. They say goodbye, and Vienna runs to the bathroom.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: And I think that's where it all hit my body. And it's almost like I'd been holding my breath the whole time.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah. What's it like when it's hitting your body? What does it feel like?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: [EXHALES] The stress of all the detail was almost being downloaded to my body.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Oh, dear. Oh, dear. [CRYING] Oh, dear. Oh, no.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna waits a minute to make sure Justin's really gone, and then heads upstairs to the hotel room to meet up with her sister, Shawnessy, and the undercover team.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I knock on the door. Somebody opens it. And they are all practically at the door. They're as close as the door as they physically all could be. And it was so visible on everyone--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: What does their face look like? Yeah.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: [SIGHS] It's like celebration, like shock and awe, and whoa, you did it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Vienna pulled it off. The meeting really couldn't have been more of a success. This wire recording ended up being the central piece of evidence used in court. Justin is charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of voyeurism, and one count of administering a stupefying drug. He pleads guilty to all but the drug charge. Vienna assumes he did this to try to avoid losing his vet license.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Justin ended up getting a sentence of two years minus a day of house arrest, where he was still allowed to leave the house for work and church and errands. The crown counsel appealed. The Court of Appeals eventually overruled the original sentence, and Justin had to serve out his term in federal prison, though, after just six months in prison, Justin was granted parole.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Whatever you think of his sentence, this result is exceptionally rare. The vast majority of sexual assaults are, of course, never reported to the police. And in Canada, of the cases that are reported and make it to court, only about 6% result in jail time for the perpetrator. So those are the sort of satisfying legal consequences.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But remember, Vienna went into this because ever since Justin assaulted her, she'd had this unsettled feeling, this itch to know what happened to her. And now that she knows, Vienna says that for the first time since that night, she's able to not think about what happened to her. She used to think about it all the time.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: It's kind of crazy how captive I was to everything that was done to me, the not knowing and how much it-- yeah, it dictated so much of my life. And now, I don't have to worry about it anymore. And I'm tired. And I'm just going to let the rest be.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And then there's the last thing Vienna was hoping to get out of all of this. In some ways, it was the thing she wanted most. And that's getting her sister Sunny back. After the trial, once Vienna's parents learned the full extent of what Justin did to her, they cut Justin out. But Sunny is still married to him. Vienna had thought that if she could get Justin to lay out exactly what he did to her with all the graphic details, and if Sunny could hear that version of the story--

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: My hope was that she would be able to [SIGHS] empathize, be able to be my sister, instead of being his wife. I thought if she knew the truth, it would change everything.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But as far as Vienna knows, Sunny never heard the tape. She served as a witness for Justin in the trial, and so was kept out of the courtroom until it was her time to be called to the stand, which meant she missed all the wire tape that Vienna's lawyers played in court. I reached out to Sunny and Justin multiple times. I never heard back.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It must be frustrating to do such a good job at getting the facts of what happened that night, and then for the facts to do nothing to persuade the person you were trying to convince the most that something did happen.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, it's really hard in terms of, look, I did this for you, and you don't want to see it. But also, I mean, I can't have a relationship if she can't recognize what happened or what was done to me. It's--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: I want a relationship with my sister. I love her deeply, but also, I'm not OK with her staying married to him. So I--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah. They would need to break up in order for you to have a meaningfully close relationship with her again.

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Do you hold out any hope of that happening?

segments.speaker: Vienna Luke
segments.text: Yeah. As much as I need to move on and find peace, I always hold on to a little bit of hope.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: After Vienna's conversation with Justin, she drove home, exhaustion taking over as the adrenaline started to recede. She still had the goodie bag from Sunny. Vienna's partner, Jordan, thought she should get rid of it, throw the stuff away. But she didn't want to. She used to love baking cookies with Sunny. Maybe this was Sunny's oblique way of saying, I know everything is messed up. I know I chose Justin over you. I know things won't ever be the same. But I'm still here, and I still love you. That's what Vienna would like to believe, anyway. So she unwrapped the cookies and ate them.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This story first came to us from the CBC. They made a whole four-part series about Vienna, called Personally-- Agent Layla. Their story goes far beyond the tape you heard today. There's a link to their series on our website, so go take a listen. If you've experienced sexual assault and want to talk to somebody, you can reach out to the National Sexual Assault Hotline, 1-800-656-HOPE.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Coming up, a person passes a test they had no idea they were taking. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Aviva DeKornfeld, sitting in for Ira Glass. Today's show, The Missing Minutes. We've arrived at Act Two of our show, Act Two, Unknown Unknowns. So there's information you know you don't know. But then there's all the other stuff, stuff that just doesn't quite make sense, but you don't know why. You feel like you're missing something. So you hope that one day, it'll all be explained and finally made clear. This last story is a short piece of fiction about what that day might be like. It's by Miranda July. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: Someone is getting excited. Somebody, somewhere, is shaking with excitement because something tremendous is about to happen to this person. This person has dressed for the occasion. This person's hoped and dreamed. And now it is really happening, and this person can hardly believe it. But believing is not an issue here. It is really, really happening.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: It involves stepping forward and bowing. Possibly, there is some kneeling, such as when one is knighted. One is almost never knighted. But this person may kneel and receive a tap on each shoulder with a sword. Or, more likely, this person will be in a car, or a store, or under a vinyl canopy when it happens, or online, or on the phone. It could be an email, Re-- Your Knighthood, or a long, laughing, rambling phone message in which every person this person has ever known is talking on a speakerphone, and they are all saying, you have passed the test. It was all just a test. We were only kidding. Real life is so much better than that.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person is laughing out loud with relief and playing the message back to get the address of the place where every person this person has ever known is waiting to hug this person and bring her into the fold of life. It is really exciting. And it's not just a dream. It's real.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: They are all waiting by a picnic table in a park this person has driven past many times before. There they are. It's everyone. There are balloons taped to the benches. And the girl this person used to stand next to at the bus stop is waving a streamer. Everyone is smiling. For a moment, this person is almost creeped out by the scene. But it would be so like this person to become depressed on the happiest day ever, so this person bucks up and joins the crowd.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: Teachers of subjects that this person wasn't even good at are kissing this person and renouncing the very subjects they taught. Math teachers are saying that math was just a funny way of saying, I love you. But now they are simply saying it-- I love you. And the chemistry and PE teachers are also saying it. And this person can tell they really mean it. It's totally amazing.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: Certain jerks and idiots and assholes appear from time to time, and it's as if they've had plastic surgery. Their faces are disfigured with love. The handsome assholes are plain and kind. And the ugly jerks are sweet, and they're folding this person's sweater and putting it somewhere where it won't get dirty. Best of all, every person this person has ever loved is there, even the ones who got away. They hold this person's hand and tell this person how hard it was to pretend to get mad and drive off and never come back.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person almost can't believe it. It seemed so real. This person's heart was broken and has healed, and now this person hardly knows what to think. This person is almost mad. But everyone soothes this person. Everyone explains that it was absolutely necessary to know how strong this person was.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: Oh, look, there's the doctor who prescribed the medicine that made this person temporarily blind, and the man who paid this person $2,000 to have sex with him three times when this person was very broke. Both these men are in attendance. They seem to know each other. They both have little medals that they're pinning on this person. They are badges of great honor and strength. The badges sparkle in the sunlight, and everyone cheers.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person suddenly feels the need to check her post office box. It is an old habit. And even if everything's going to be terrific from now on, this person still wants mail. This person says she'll be right back, and everyone this person has ever known says, fine, take your time. This person gets in her car and drives to the post office and opens the box, and there is nothing, even though it is Tuesday, which is a famously good day for mail.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person is so disappointed, this person gets back in the car and, having completely forgotten about the picnic, drives home and checks the voicemail, and there are no new messages, just the old one about passing the test and life being better. There are no emails either, probably because everyone is at the picnic. This person can't seem to go back to the picnic. This person realizes that staying home means blowing off everyone this person has ever known. But the desire to stay in is very strong. This person wants to run a bath and then read in bed.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: In the bathtub, this person pushes the bubbles around and listens to the sound of millions of them popping at once. This person pushes the bubbles onto their breasts and makes weird shapes with the foam. By now, everyone must have realized that this person is not coming back to the picnic. Everyone was wrong. This person is not who they thought this person was.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person plunges underwater. This person can stay underwater for an impressively long time, but only in a bathtub. This person wonders if there will ever be an Olympic contest for holding your breath under bathwater. If there were such a contest, this person would surely win it. An Olympic medal might redeem this person in the eyes of everyone this person has ever known. But no such contest exists, so there will be no redeeming.

segments.speaker: Miranda July
segments.text: This person mourns the fact that she has ruined her one chance to be loved by everyone. As this person climbs into bed, the weight of this tragedy seems to bear down upon this person's chest. And it is a comforting weight, almost human in heft. This person sighs. This person's eyes begin to close. This person sleeps.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Miranda July. She is the author of the book All Fours, which is the only book that I, upon completing, flipped over and immediately started reading again. I can't recommend it enough. Miranda also has a Substack called, appropriately, Miranda July. Check it out.
